title: ARC – Antiresorptive Concept: Evaluation of Complication Rates and Quality of Life in an Integrated Dental and Orthopedic Care Pathway
summary:
Why is this study being conducted?
Femoral neck fractures are common injuries and represent a major challenge in orthopedic care. Surgical treatment is required to enable early mobilization and pain relief.

A femoral neck fracture is considered a fragility (index) fracture, meaning that it often indicates the presence of underlying osteoporosis. Osteoporosis weakens the bones and increases the risk of future fractures. Therefore, patients are usually offered anti-osteoporotic medication after surgery to strengthen bone and reduce the risk of subsequent fractures.

Following surgery, patients are generally advised to receive long-term anti-osteoporotic treatment. This treatment may be initiated and monitored either by our department or by a physician specializing in metabolic bone diseases (osteologist).

Like all medications, antiresorptive therapy may cause side effects. Although rare, one serious complication is medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw (MRONJ), a condition in which part of the jawbone loses its blood supply and becomes necrotic. For this reason, careful dental assessment before treatment initiation and regular dental follow-up during therapy are strongly recommended.

The aim of this study is to evaluate patients' quality of life following treatment for a femoral neck fracture, with particular focus on:

oral health and oral health-related quality of life,
general health-related quality of life, and
satisfaction with the treated hip joint.

In addition, we aim to investigate whether patients experience subsequent fractures while receiving anti-osteoporotic therapy.

Participants will attend annual follow-up visits at the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery for a total of three years. During these visits, dental health will be assessed to determine whether oral health has deteriorated or whether teeth require extraction. Treatment recommendations will be provided to the participant's general dentist where appropriate. Participants will also complete several validated questionnaires assessing different aspects of quality of life.

What does participation involve?

Participation in this study will last approximately three years and includes three annual follow-up visits.

During the initial hospital admission, participants will undergo a dental examination to assess their oral health. If teeth requiring treatment or extraction are identified, appropriate dental treatment should be completed before anti-osteoporotic medication is initiated whenever clinically feasible.

Following discharge, participants will be invited to attend the outpatient clinic of the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery once each year. During these visits, changes in oral health will be assessed. The dental examination takes approximately 10 minutes. Based on the findings, our department will provide treatment recommendations to the participant's general dentist. If participants have no or only limited access to outpatient dental care, treatment can be provided by our department.

Participants will also be asked to complete several questionnaires assessing:

oral health-related quality of life,
general health-related quality of life, and
hip-related symptoms and function.

Completing these questionnaires takes approximately 30 minutes.

At each annual visit, participants will additionally be asked whether they have experienced any new fractures or required hospital admission since their previous assessment.

What happens if an unexpected finding is discovered?

During the course of this study, findings unrelated to the study objectives may occasionally be identified. For example, abnormalities that could indicate oral cancer or another medical condition may be detected. These are referred to as incidental findings.

Participants may decide whether they wish to be informed about such incidental findings. This decision will not affect their medical care or their participation in the study.

Please note that receiving information about an incidental finding may have both advantages and disadvantages. While early detection may facilitate timely medical evaluation and treatment, learning about a previously unknown condition may also cause anxiety or emotional distress. In addition, knowledge of certain diseases or disease risks may influence future applications for private health insurance, life insurance, disability insurance, or other insurance policies that require disclosure of medical information. This may affect insurance eligibility or policy conditions.

Participants are therefore encouraged to consider carefully whether they wish to receive information about incidental findings.

Are there any benefits from participating?

Participation in this study does not provide access to any experimental medical treatment.

However, participants may benefit from regular dental examinations that facilitate early detection and treatment of oral health problems. The annual follow-up visits also include assessment of hip function and satisfaction following surgery.

Furthermore, the knowledge gained from this study may contribute to improving the future care of patients with femoral neck fractures and osteoporosis, helping to optimize treatment strategies and reduce the risk of subsequent fractures.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Patients with femoral neck fractures treated with endoprosthetic reconstruction
Low-energy (fragility) fractures
Patients with an indication for initiation of specific anti-osteoporotic therapy or patients already receiving established specific anti-osteoporotic treatment
Exclusion criteria:
-Patients <18 years of age
-Femoral neck fractures requiring surgical treatment other than the aforementioned endoprosthetic procedure
-Other types of proximal femoral fractures (e.g., pertrochanteric fractures)
-Confirmed pathological fractures due to an underlying malignant disease
-Femoral neck fractures resulting from high-energy trauma
-Patients with insufficient German language skills to fully understand the study information and procedures
-Refusal to participate in the study
-Inability or unwillingness to comply with study procedures, including refusal of dental examination
